title: Tolosa v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A.
summary: The alleged oral promise to delay foreclosure fell within the Texas loan-agreement writing requirement, and the pleaded reliance did not satisfy the specific estoppel exception applied by the court.
notes: The suit (S.D. Tex., No. 4:11-cv-03484, 2011) pleaded fraud, wrongful foreclosure, slander of title, promissory estoppel, unreasonable collection and an accounting; HSBC's motion argued that every claim rested on the alleged oral promise and so was barred by the Texas statute of frauds for loan agreements.

sections.Parties: The Tolosas, borrowers whose home had been foreclosed upon, sued HSBC Bank USA. The federal district court addressed HSBC’s motion to dismiss after removal from Texas state court.
sections.Material Facts:
The borrowers obtained a $276,000 loan to purchase property in Sugar Land, Texas. A promissory note documented the loan, and a deed of trust secured it. After default, the property was sold at foreclosure in April 2011. The borrowers alleged that the bank had promised not to foreclose while a loan modification was being reviewed.

They sued in September to delay eviction and asserted several theories, including fraud and promissory estoppel. Their response to dismissal relied in part on a state temporary restraining order and on the alleged promise to delay foreclosure. They did not allege a promise by the bank to sign a writing that would meet the statute’s requirements.
sections.Procedural History: The state action was removed on diversity grounds. The Southern District of Texas granted HSBC’s motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The assigned excerpt explains the statute-of-frauds and promissory-estoppel analysis rather than supplying a complete discussion of every pleaded theory.
sections.Issue: Could the borrowers enforce the alleged oral accommodation, directly or through promissory estoppel, despite the Texas statute governing loan agreements exceeding $50,000?
sections.Holding: No on the allegations presented. A promise to delay foreclosure was a financial accommodation within the statute, and the borrowers had not pleaded the promise to sign a compliant writing required by the Texas estoppel rule the court applied.
sections.Reasoning:
The statute reached more than the initial advance of money. Its definition included commitments to delay repayment or make financial accommodations. The alleged foreclosure delay therefore belonged within the writing requirement, despite being framed as a promise made during later modification discussions.

The borrowers could not avoid that requirement simply by relabeling the promise as promissory estoppel. The particular Texas doctrine described in the opinion required a promise to sign a writing satisfying the statute. That allegation was missing. The editors then use the case to distinguish making a contract from proving the form necessary to enforce it, and discuss the statute’s separate notice provisions. Those notes raise additional questions about notice and fairness; the opinion does not find a notice violation on these facts.

priorVersions.summary: The alleged oral foreclosure assurance failed under the Texas loan-writing requirement applied in the excerpt; the pleaded facts did not fit its narrow estoppel exception.
priorVersions.notes: Scope: the account follows the casebook’s excerpt at pp. 372–374. The $50,000 threshold and the exception are reported as the law used in that decision, not verified as a current nationwide rule. The following notes introduce statutory coverage, sufficiency of a writing, and exceptions as separate inquiries.

sections.Parties: The borrowers, including Tolosa, sued HSBC concerning a home mortgage and the handling of a possible loan modification.
sections.Material Facts: The loan was approximately $276,000. After default, the borrowers alleged an oral assurance that foreclosure would be delayed while modification was considered. They sought to enforce that assurance despite the absence of the required signed writing.
sections.Procedural History: The court resolved the pleaded claim at the dismissal stage under Rule 12(b)(6). It applied the Texas statutory writing requirement for loan agreements exceeding $50,000 and rejected the asserted route around it.
sections.Issue: Could the borrowers enforce the alleged oral loan-related assurance, or avoid the writing requirement through promissory estoppel?
sections.Holding: The pleading did not establish an enforceable agreement under the applicable writing rule. The promissory-estoppel exception discussed by the court required a promise to sign an existing writing satisfying the statute; that promise was not alleged.
sections.Reasoning: The court classifies the undertaking within the covered loan transaction and then examines the exception asserted. An assurance to forbear is different from a promise to execute a statute-compliant writing. The decision illustrates the need to identify the particular jurisdiction’s statute and exceptions rather than invoke a general conception of fairness or § 90 alone.

sources.label: Farnsworth et al., Contracts: Cases and Materials, 10th ed. (2023), pp. 372–375. Open assigned page 372.

learning.why: This is a useful limit on any blanket statement that reliance makes a promise enforceable. Identify the governing statute and the jurisdiction’s exception before relying on § 90 in the abstract.

topics.statute-frauds: A specific statute requires a signed writing for the accommodation.
topics.promissory-estoppel: The court applies a jurisdiction-specific limit to reliance as a response to a writing requirement.
topics.modification: Later promises about an existing loan can fall within the same statutory form requirement.
topics.rest90: The court applied the narrow Texas version of promissory estoppel as a statute-of-frauds exception (a promise to sign a compliant writing), which contrasts with the broader Restatement section 90/139 approach.
